title: Know Thy Place
paragraphs: 1. KNOW THY PLACE.
By Trevor Swistchew (2026)
God walked into the celestial courtroom like He owned the joint, because He did. His look filled the room.

The audience knew their mortality stared them in the face. God did not wait or sit. He just stood there, coat slung over His shoulder, jaw set like an old Chicago Don who'd spent eternity dealing with idiots who thought they could outsmart Him.

“Alright,” He said, voice rolling through the chamber like a freight train on a cold Chicago night. “We're clearing this up right now. All property? Theft. Every inch. Every deed. Every shiny little certificate you clowns wave around like it means something. It's Mine. I built the universe. I laid the foundations. I lit the stars. You think you own a condo? You don't even own the atoms in your own damn bones.”
A few lawyers tried shuffling papers, but God flicked His fingers and every brief turned into a slice of cold pizza.
“Don't insult Me with paperwork,” He said. “I was doing contracts before your species figured out how to stop drooling.”
One attorney stood up, shaking like a kid caught stealing cannoli. “ Your Honour surely humanity has rights?”

God leaned in, eyes narrowing like headlights on a dark Chicago street. “Kid, nobody fucks with My universe. Nobody. You try to claim ownership of something I made? That's like trying to sell Me My own car. You know what that makes you? A clown. A cosmic clown. And I don't tolerate clowns.”
The judge tried to bang the gavel, but God raised a hand. The gavel turned into a meatball. A good one. “Sit down, Your Honour,” God said. “This ain't your show.”
Then He turned to humanity, all of them, every last one, standing there like they'd been dragged into court for the biggest eviction notice in cosmic history.

“You people,” God said, “you build fences, you draw lines, you slap your names on things like toddlers claiming chairs. You fight wars over dirt. Dirt. I made galaxies, and you're out here stabbing each other over who gets the corner lot with the nice view. You know what that is? Embarrassing. For Me.”
He paced, hands behind His back, coat swinging like a cape. “I gave you a whole universe. A whole cosmic playground. And you turned it into a yard sale.”

A billionaire opened his mouth. God didn't even look at him. “Don't start,” He said. “You're the worst. You hoard My stuff like a raccoon with a shiny spoon. You build towers to your own ego and call it success. You think wealth makes you clever. It doesn't. It just makes you loud.”

God stopped. Looked straight at humanity. “So here's the ruling. Final. Eternal. No appeals. You don't own anything. Not the land. Not the sky. Not the water. Not the gold. Not the oil. Not the fancy penthouse you brag about. It's Mine. Always was. Always will be. I let you use My universe. I let you live in it. I let you breathe My air. I let you walk around like you're big shots. But don't forget who the landlord is. And don't forget the rent. The rent is decency. The rent is humility. The rent is not acting like a suit‑stuffed jackass who thinks profit is a personality.”
He turned to leave, coat swinging, cosmic swagger in every step. At the door, He paused.
“Moral of the story,” He said, voice dropping low and final. “If you're a wannabe capitalist bastard who thinks you own the world, remember this: you're just borrowing it. And I don't lend to fools.”
Then He walked out, and the courtroom lights flickered like they'd just been told the truth for the first time.

title: The Explanation of the Universe
paragraphs: THE EXPLANATION OF THE UNIVERSE
(Part 1  The Birth of Motion)

The universe begins in a state beyond anything language can capture. Before the first moment there is no space to contain distance, no time to measure duration, no matter to hold form, no energy to carry movement. There is only a compressed tension without shape, a potential without direction, a waiting that cannot be called waiting because waiting requires time. In that primordial condition, nothing exists except the possibility of existence. It is a state without silence, because silence needs a medium. It is a state without darkness, because darkness needs a place where light could be absent. It is a state without stillness, because stillness is the absence of motion, and motion has not yet been invented.

When the universe ignites in the event humans later name the Big Bang, it is not an explosion inside a pre‑existing void. It is the creation of the void itself. Space unfolds. Time begins. Energy surges outward. Matter condenses. The first truth of reality reveals itself instantly: everything moves. Nothing remains fixed. Change is not an accessory to existence; it is the foundation upon which existence stands. If a creator exists, that creator does not choose stillness. A static universe would collapse under its own emptiness, incapable of forming stars, incapable of producing planets incapable of generating the delicate and brutal machinery of life. Change is the only permanent, and everything else is a temporary expression of that permanence.

As the newborn universe expands, it cools enough for particles to combine. Hydrogen and helium gather into vast clouds pulled together by gravity until they ignite into stars. These stars burn with unimaginable intensity, forging heavier elements in their cores. When they exhaust their fuel, they die in spectacular collapses and explosions, scattering their enriched matter across the cosmos. Every planet, every ocean, every mountain, every living creature is built from the remnants of ancient stellar deaths. Even the atoms in human bodies were forged in stars that lived and died long before Earth existed. Death is not the opposite of life; it is the engine that makes life possible. Without the death of stars there would be no carbon, no oxygen, no iron, no chemistry capable of supporting anything alive. The universe writes its story through endings.

On one small world orbiting an ordinary star, matter arranges itself into forms capable of self‑replication. Life begins not as a miracle but as a consequence of chemistry and change. The earliest organisms are simple, fragile, unaware, but they carry within them the essential requirement of all life: they must consume to survive. To grow, they must take in matter. To take in matter, they must dismantle something else. Even the first microbes survive by breaking down molecules around them. Life cannot exist without consumption, and consumption cannot exist without destruction. A painless universe is impossible because life itself is built on the transformation of matter, and transformation is never gentle.

As life evolves, it becomes more intricate. Organisms develop senses, movement, strategies, and eventually consciousness. Yet the requirement remains unchanged: to live, something must be consumed. Plants absorb sunlight, water, minerals, and kill microbes in the soil. Animals consume plants, other animals, or both. Even the most advanced alien intelligence imaginable would still need energy, still need matter, still need to dismantle something to sustain itself. Life is not a peaceful arrangement; it is a dynamic exchange built on the tension between creation and destruction. Pain emerges as a necessary feedback system, the warning signal that keeps organisms alive. Without pain, creatures would not avoid danger, would not learn, would not adapt. Pain is not cruelty; it is information.

Death becomes the simplest and most practical solution to the problem of life. If organisms did not die, ecosystems would collapse under infinite accumulation. Resources would be consumed without renewal. Evolution would freeze. Adaptation would stop. The first generation of life would choke all future generations out of existence. Death clears space. Death recycles matter. Death allows the universe to reuse what it has already created. Without death, life would be a brief, catastrophic burst that ends almost immediately. With death, life becomes a continuous unfolding, a chain of transformations stretching across billions of years.

Human beings arrive late in this cosmic story, carrying the same biological requirements as every other creature. They must eat, they must grow, they must consume. But unlike other animals, humans develop language, imagination, and the ability to create explanations. Faced with the vastness of existence, they invent stories to make sense of what they cannot yet understand. They create gods to explain storms, spirits to explain illness, rituals to explain death. These stories are not foolish; they are attempts to impose meaning on a world that does not speak in human terms. Sin emerges as a human invention, a tool for regulating behaviour, a way to prevent the tribe from collapsing into violence. It is not a cosmic truth. It is a social mechanism disguised as divine law.

As human thought expands, the limitations of early explanations become impossible to ignore. The universe is too vast, too ancient, too intricate to fit inside the boundaries of myth. Humans discover that the Earth is not the centre of creation. They discover that the stars are suns. They discover that galaxies stretch across unimaginable distances. They discover that time itself is woven into the fabric of space. They discover that the universe is not fixed but expanding, not stable but shifting, not orderly but constantly rearranging itself. The old stories of sin and divine judgement cannot contain the scale of this reality.

Humanity begins to awaken to the true nature of existence. They learn that matter is made of atoms, that atoms are made of particles, that particles are made of energy. They learn that life is built from the same elements that form stars. They learn that consciousness is not a gift from the gods but an emergent property of matter arranged in complex patterns. They learn that death is not a punishment but a structural necessity. They learn that pain is not cruelty but information. They learn that consumption is not sin but biology. They learn that change is not chaos but the foundation of reality.

The more humans learn, the more they realise that the universe does not operate on human rules. It does not enforce morality. It does not prevent suffering. It does not intervene to stop destruction. It simply moves. It transforms. It recycles. It evolves. Everything rises, falls, breaks, heals, dies, and begins again. Change is the constant. Death is the mechanism. Life is the expression. Meaning is the result.
